#### Reference: `docs/CLUB_2026-10-28.md`

<!-- TB_REFERENCE {"path": "docs/CLUB_2026-10-28.md", "sha256": "4e2e3d533b2f94a65e4e96190ec30a7e3a920dfaafe077be536a21c4d2d8e346", "trailing_newline": true} -->
````````markdown
# Club session, 28 Oct 2026: what the raw recordings show

15 raw-stream CSV exports from the app (`data/club-2026-10-28/`, kept local, not in git). They cover about 86 minutes,
from 19:15 to 21:22 Pacific. They were made before impact mode (firmware 1.5), so this is raw streaming on a real
court. IMU only: the CSV has no mic data, so the sweet-spot model can't be checked here.

Reproduce:

```bash
python3 tools/csv_session_stats.py data/club-2026-10-28
```

## Findings

**1. Only about 17% of the 1 kHz stream arrived (13–30% per recording).** Samples come in runs of 8 or 16 (one or
two packets), separated by gaps of 17–25 ms. Median throughput was 214 samples/s, the 10th percentile 64 and the
90th 338. That is about one 8-sample packet per connection interval, far below what the link should carry. Earlier
estimates of a quarter to a third lost were optimistic: on court it was closer to four fifths. This alone rules out
judging shot quality from raw-stream recordings, and it confirms the switch to impact mode.

**2. Impact-mode windows will take about 2 s to deliver.** A 448-sample window at the measured median throughput takes
about 2.1 s. In these sessions, 16% of consecutive high-g events came less than 1.8 s apart, and the 10th percentile
was 1.0 s. Impact mode still sends a hit notification for each of these, but a window can't start while the previous
one is still sending. So expect roughly 1 window in 6 to be missing during fast exchanges, unless throughput
improves. Worth logging on court: `windowBusy` drops, plus the connection interval the phone actually grants (the
status line already prints it).

**3. The gyro clipped at ±2000 dps on court, although the app asks for ±4000.** 8 of the 12 recordings that have data
show gyro samples flat-topped at exactly 34.87 rad/s, which is the int16 limit at 16.4 LSB/dps. At ±4000 dps
the ceiling would be 69.7 rad/s. So during those swings the IMU was in its ±2000 dps range. On paper the code path
looks right: the app writes `gyroRange 1` on connect, the firmware switches between packets and flags the packets,
and the app decodes the flag. So check this on the hardware next. Connect over USB serial during a session and
read the status line, which prints `2000` or `4000`. Possible causes: an older firmware on the racket that night,
or a reconnect path that skips characteristic discovery and so never resends the command. None of the received
samples within 150 ms of a detected hit were clipped. The clipped samples come from the fastest swings, most likely
serves and swings whose impact fell in a gap. Swing speed and spin on those shots will read low.

*Follow-up (firmware 1.6):* ST's driver changes the gyro full scale only with the gyro powered down. Our firmware
wrote CTRL6 with the gyro running, the most likely reason the switch didn't take effect. Firmware 1.6 switches
the range ST's way and checks the readback. It also boots at ±4000 and returns there on disconnect, so the range
no longer depends on the app's command arriving. Each recording now gets a `.link.json` with the gyro range and
packet counts, so the next session will show which range was really in use.

**4. Accel low-g saturates on every hard hit (expected).** ±16 g clips on most hits. The high-g channel covers them,
with a median event peak of 21 g, 90th percentile 85 g and a maximum of 233 g (vector). On the wire, high-g is
sent at the app's default ±200 g range, although the sensor reads ±320 g. One sample in the first recording hit
200.7 g on the face-normal axis, and two others peaked at 184–187 g. A hard serve or frame hit will clip at
200 g, so consider the 400 g wire range (`h3lisRange` 3), at the cost of half the resolution. That cost is
negligible in practice: the 400 g step is 0.195 g, while the sensor's noise at rest is 0.35 g RMS and the median
post-impact ring is 3.9 g. The 200 g limit comes from sending high-g as old H3LIS 12-bit counts, not from the
sensor, which reads ±320 g at 10.4 mg per step.

**5. Session hygiene.** 3 of the 15 files are empty (0–16 samples). Two recordings contain a racket reboot. One of
them, `T022106`, then has a 17-minute gap, so its duration is overstated. `T024705` has no `-racket` suffix and only
low motion (a table or bench test?).

## Impact detector replay

`firmware/tools/impact_replay` on the same files finds 124 hits, against 151 high-g events in the received data.
Every window spans gaps in the recording, so these windows say nothing about the windows impact mode would produce.
They only show that the detector fires on real court motion.

| Recording | Minutes | Hits (replay) |
|---|---|---|
| T021549 | 4.0 | 11 |
| T022106 | 25.9 (17 min gap) | 11 |
| T024213 | 2.1 | 4 |
| T030114 | 2.7 | 2 |
| T031435 | 2.8 | 3 |
| T031722 | 2.2 | 8 |
| T032143 | 13.9 | 9 |
| T033619 | 22.0 | 61 |
| T035825 | 2.8 | 6 |
| T042250 | 5.4 | 9 |

## Next session at the club

- Run impact mode (firmware 1.5+) and record the delivered windows, so shot metrics can be checked on full-rate data.
- Check the gyro range on the serial status line, or add the range flag to the CSV export.
- Log the granted connection interval and packets per interval; if the phone grants 30 ms with one packet each,
  that's the 2 s window budget above.
- Record the mic as well (TennisCamera or a `.tbrec` with shots), so the ridge sweet-spot model can be checked on
  court audio.
````````

````````markdown
# Sweet-spot data collection (for Codex and humans)

Goal: labelled impact-sound clips for the on-device sweet-spot model (`ml/`). A webcam films the racket from below
while balls are thrown onto the strings; the racket mic's clips and the video share one PC clock; the ball's landing
spot is read off the video afterwards. Run everything from the repo root on the Windows PC.

## Setup (once)

```bash
pip install pyserial opencv-python numpy openai meta-sam-parser pygrabber
```

* Racket flashed with the current firmware (`firmware/`), plugged in over USB. The scripts find its serial port
  and the external USB webcam (not the laptop camera) on their own; override with `--port COMx` / `--camera N`.
* Optional SAM pre-fill and scaling: put `MUSE_API_KEY=...` in the repo-root `.env` (git-ignored). SAM calls upload
  video frames (including faces) to Meta and cost money (about $2.50 per 1,000 images); the scripts print the
  cost and ask first. Do not print or commit the key.
* Racket held horizontal, head up, still in frame; balls thrown down onto the strings; webcam below looking up.
  Do not handle the racket while recording.

### Adaptive decay capture (new firmware)

Flash the updated firmware before collecting new samples (`pio run -e xiao_esp32c3 -t upload` in `firmware/`).
Collection retains 4 ms before the trigger and continues for 128 ms after the last sample whose absolute
value is at least 30000 (near full scale). If no sample reaches that level, it retains 128 ms after the trigger.
Recording stops at 1 second after the trigger even if clipping continues. The threshold is a conservative
clipping indicator; it does not prove that the microphone has recovered from all distortion.

First record five test impacts. Leave at least two seconds between drops during this check. The terminal
shows each clip's duration. Inspect the tail before collecting the full batch:

```powershell
python tools/listen_clip.py data/sessions/<session>/clips/clip-0001.i16 --tail-only
```

Open the resulting `.tail.wav` to hear the decay after the final near-full-scale sample. The tool also prints
how much tail remains. If it reports less than 128 ms, the recording reached the limit (or used older firmware).
Do not collect the full batch until the test confirms a usable decay recording.

`clips.csv` now includes `impact_t_s` and `samples`. The impact time is estimated from the firmware's trigger
age when it sends metadata, before the audio payload. SAM and the labeller use this estimate so longer clips
do not shift their initial video frame. USB buffering can still introduce timing error; check contact manually.
Older sessions retain the previous timing estimate.

The existing deployed model still uses the initial 512 samples (32 ms). Training accepts extended recordings
but explicitly reports that it uses only this initial window. The complete tail stays in the source clip for
decay analysis and a later model change. Old 32 ms clips cannot supply the missing decay tail.

## 1. Record a session

```bash
python3 tools/collect_session.py --name <note>
```

Writes `data/sessions/<time>-<note>/`: `video.avi`, `frames.csv`, `clips.csv`, `clips/*.i16`. Press `q` in the
preview window to stop. The preview flashes green on each impact; the terminal marks `** CLIPPED` when the mic
saturated (most throws do; the clips are still saved).

## 2. Label from the video

```bash
python3 tools/label_video.py data/sessions/<session>
```

* First run: calibrate. Scrub (`a`/`d` 1 frame, `w`/`s` 5, `j`/`k` 60) to a frame with the racket clear, click the
  string-bed centre, click a point toward the tip, type its distance in cm in the terminal. Press `c` to redo.
* Per impact: step to the frame the ball touches the strings; click the ball, then the string-bed centre (marks are
  cleared when you step frames); Enter accepts, `x` discards (handling noise, bounces, double triggers), `b` or
  Ctrl+Z goes back, `q` saves and quits. Progress is saved after every label; `--redo` relabels everything.
* Output: `labels.csv` (`file,dist_cm`, what `ml/train.py` reads), `positions.csv`, `discarded.txt`.

## 3. Optional: SAM pre-fill (before step 2) and scaling (after)

```bash
python3 tools/sam_prefill.py data/sessions/<session> --probe     # one frame, check the boxes in sam_probe.jpg
python3 tools/sam_prefill.py data/sessions/<session>             # all impacts, asks before uploading
python3 tools/sam_scale.py   data/sessions/<session>             # after labelling
```

`sam_prefill.py` pre-fills the ball and racket-head clicks in the labeller. `sam_scale.py` rescales every label from
the racket's string-bed area (set to 100 in^2, change with `--head-area`) so racket movement toward or away from
the camera is accounted for. It supersedes `tools/sam_refine.py`. Originals stay in `labels_unscaled.csv`.

## 4. Train

```bash
python3 ml/train.py --real data/sessions/<session>
```

`ml/train.py --real` reads one folder (`labels.csv` plus the clips it names). To combine sessions, copy clips and
labels into one folder first. Use `--real-only` once there are roughly 300 or more real clips. Then rebuild and flash
the firmware (`pio run -t upload` in `firmware/`) and run `python3 ml/test_parity.py`. Keep one whole session
out of training as a test set.

## Known issues

* The mic (INMP441) saturates on most throws. Check `** CLIPPED` and the `peak=` values; attenuating the mic
  mechanically would help. Decay and attack features are unreliable on clipped clips.
* The firmware prints samples big-endian; the scripts convert them to little-endian `.i16`. Clips recorded earlier on
  2026-10-27 were byte-swapped and repaired in place (a `byteswap_fixed` marker file in a session folder shows it).
* Only the first ~100 labelled impacts exist so far; expect to need about 300 to 500 for a useful model.

## Phone + racket sessions (IMU swing data, ball ground truth)

For the IMU swing model: the iPhone app `TennisRobot/ios/TennisCamera` films at 240 fps, detects the ball, and
connects to the racket over BLE itself, so the camera frames and racket IMU packets are stamped on one clock.

1. Build the app (`xcodegen generate` in `TennisRobot/ios/TennisCamera`, new files were added; then run it on the
   phone). Allow camera and Bluetooth. Power the racket; the app finds it by its service UUID.
2. Phone on a tripod to the side, about 3 m from you, square to the swing plane, ball and racket in frame.
3. **Start capture**, wait for `racket: connected` and `imu` near 125 pkt/s (1 kHz samples, 8 per packet) with few lost, then **Record session**. Press **Mark** while knocking the racket on something in view (a sync point).
   **Stop recording** when done. Keep "Save 240 fps video" on unless frames drop; it needs about 2 GB per 10 minutes.
4. Copy `Files > On My iPhone > TennisCamera > sessions/<stamp>` to `data/phone/<stamp>` on the PC.
5. `python tools/phone_session.py data/phone/<stamp>` fits the racket-to-phone clock (offset, drift) and refines it
   from ball contacts; it writes `sync.json`, `imu_aligned.npz` and `ball_track.csv`. `--plot` shows the alignment.
   `python tools/test_phone_session.py` checks the aligner on synthetic data.

Hit gently into the blanket: a soft ball may not reach the 10 g impact threshold (use `--threshold 4`).

## In-app sweet-spot check (no PC needed)

Racket tab → **Calibrate racket…** ends with an optional sweet-spot check: tape a 3×3 grid on the strings (5 cm
across, 6 cm along), tap a square in the app, drop a ball on it. The center square is the sweet spot. The app pairs
each drop with the racket's on-device verdict and its own motion-sensor estimate, shows how often the model was right
(sweet and off-center separately), and saves `Calibration/sweetspot-check-<time>.csv` (Files app on iPhone, or the
share button). `dist_cm` matches `labels.csv`. It holds no audio, so it measures the deployed model on hardware but
cannot train it; use the webcam flow above for training clips.

````````

````````markdown
# Demo script (3 minutes)

**Before going on:** Mac app open full screen on the projector, racket connected (or Simulator as backup), signed in
on the Mac and iPhone (Muse needs the network), Watch on the presenter's non-playing wrist, a ball and a hanging blanket or a partner.

1. **The fork (15 s).** "We forked an open-source smart racket that sent one acceleration number over Wi-Fi and lit a
   red or green LED. We kept its idea and rebuilt everything around it." Show `legacy/` and the fork badge on GitHub.
2. **The trick: the racket (60 s).**
   - Pick up the racket: the 3D racket on screen moves with it. Hit **Recenter** first.
   - Start a session from the **Watch** (it also starts a Tennis workout).
   - Hit a ball into the blanket: the shot card pops up with ball speed, swing speed, spin, face angle, and the dot
     where the ball hit the strings. The card edge flashes **green** for the sweet spot, **red** for a mishit (the
     original project's LEDs, reborn). The Watch taps your wrist the same way.
   - Mention the hardware: two IMUs (gyro + 200 g accelerometer) streaming 1,000 samples/s from inside the handle.
3. **The treat: analytics (60 s).**
   - End the session on the Watch → History: shot mix, impact heat map per stroke, speed over the session.
   - Tap **Ask Muse**: Muse Spark (Meta) pulls the session through tools and writes the report.
   - Insights → Muse → ask "What's my weakest stroke?" and "Plan my next drill". Muse calls the tools live
     (shots, racket sensors, notes, the what-if simulator); point out the "Muse remembered…" line.
4. **How accurate? (30 s).** Show the slide comparing app numbers with 240 fps slow-mo measurements.

**If Bluetooth fails:** Racket tab → Recorder → replay a recorded session (it plays exactly like the live racket), or
switch the source to Simulator.
````````

<!-- TB_REFERENCE {"path": "docs/EMULATOR_DATA.md", "sha256": "cb8f14726643c2ac4547bbae6c3351675a5646318c12d739692782cad957dec3", "trailing_newline": true} -->
````````markdown
# Web emulator + pro-match data spec

Judges can't swing the physical racket, so the emulator replays a real professional match
through the app's data path: SAM 3.1 tracks the racket on video, the tracks convert to the
app's session format, and a static web page plays the sessions back. Live page:
[`website/emulator.html`](../website/emulator.html) (needs `emulator_sessions.json` beside it).

## Honesty rules (non-negotiable)

1. The page always shows its provenance banner: video source, tracker, what is derived,
   and what is illustrative. No mode hides it.
2. Broadcast footage supports exactly three quantities: shot times, stroke side/kind from
   dataset labels (never guessed from pixels), and unitless swing intensity. The labelled
   match adds the hitter's racket timing from the SAM box centre (a rough 2D guide). Ball
   speed, spin, face angle, and contact point are not observable and are never presented
   as measured; the contact point is an assumed prior (see Estimated figures).
3. No real player's name is attached to measured data. Style presets are illustrative and
   say so. Never commit source footage; derived tracks + this provenance note are the artifact.
4. The committed `emulator_sessions.json` carries one entry per player, each with its own
   provenance block (video title, uploader, URL). Current file (9 players, 2,265 hits): the
   labelled Ostrava 2022 final (60 hits, real F3Tennis stroke labels and outcomes, both
   players) plus 8 broadcast matches (2,205 hits) whose stroke type, hitter and hit time are
   **predictions of the F3Tennis tsm_e2espot model** (flagged `predicted`, with its confidence),
   with SAM 3.1 racket tracks for the swing timing (611 windows, 79,945 billed frames, $15.99;
   an earlier 291-hit audio-window pass cost $5.86 and was replaced). Source videos are
   deleted after tracking. Sessions are named by match, not by one player, because both
   players' hits are in them.
5. Stroke types for those 8 matches are model predictions, never presented as labels: the shot card, the
   info panel and the footer say so. The model scored 97% (58/60) on stroke type on 60 hits of the Ostrava test
   split; accuracy on these broadcasts was not measured, and Ostrava shares its match and camera with the
   training clips, so that number is optimistic.

## Why this is a fair analogy for racket data

The emulator exercises the same pipeline the racket feeds: contact timestamps at realistic
pro cadence, forehand/backhand mix, and rally intensity flow into session totals, the shot
feed, and the what-if questions a judge can ask. What it cannot show — sensor fidelity —
is covered separately by real racket recordings, the C++/Swift/Python parity checks, and
the labeled-session tests. The emulator answers "what does the app do with a session";
the hardware evidence answers "does the racket measure truly".

## Pipeline (runs on your machine, video stays local)

```bash
# 1. Detect contacts in a clip, track +-1 s windows with SAM 3.1 (NOT the full match
#    through the API; --budget caps dollars. ~$0.20 per 1000 frames billed.)
python3 tools/sam_clip_hits.py clip.mp4 --player alcaraz --out work/alcaraz --probe
python3 tools/sam_clip_hits.py clip.mp4 --player alcaraz --out work/alcaraz \
    --max-windows 25 --budget 3 --yes

# 2. Tracks -> per-player emulator sessions (offline, no key, no network)
python3 tools/sam_players_to_emulator.py work/alcaraz work/sinner \
    -o website/emulator_sessions.json

# 2b. Labelled match (F3Tennis clips already tracked by tools/sam_f3set_video.py): real stroke
#     labels + the hitter's racket timing per hit. Replaces the 'Ostrava' entry, keeps the rest.
python3 tools/f3set_to_emulator.py data/external/f3set/sam_video --merge website/emulator_sessions.json

# 2c. Model-predicted matches (separate CUDA environment: tools/f3tennis_model/README.md):
python3 tools/f3tennis_model/detect_pros.py        # whole video at 25 fps -> <video>.ev25.json (hits, type, hitter, conf)
python3 tools/sam_model_windows.py video.mp4 video.ev25.json --player nadal --out work/nadal \
    --frames 13500 --budget 2.75 --ledger work/ledger_nadal.json --plan   # prints the cost; add --yes to spend
python3 tools/model_events_to_emulator.py work --merge website/emulator_sessions.json

# 3. Deploy: copy index.html, emulator.html, both session files and emulator/ into .website-dist/, then publish.
```

Cost control: `--budget` caps every SAM run; ledgers (`sam_video_ledger.json`) count billed
frames across runs. A full 2-hour match at 30 fps is ~216k frames (~$43) — always window
around contacts instead. Delete source video after tracking unless you are entitled to keep
it; F3Set access follows that dataset's own terms.

## What the emulator is (web page)

[`website/emulator.html`](../website/emulator.html) is a browser copy of the iPhone app's five tabs, built to
look and behave like `apple/Shared/Views`:

- **Live** — the app's real textured Yonex racket (`TennisRacket.glb`, shrunk by
  [`tools/optimize_racket_glb.py`](../tools/optimize_racket_glb.py) from 15 MB to 0.65 MB) rendered with
  three.js, the same session controls, stat tiles, shot card (green/red flash), string bed and gyro/g/Hz labels.
- **Score** — working tennis scoring (sets, tiebreaks, no-ad, match tiebreak) with the app's layout.
- **Settings** — the app's Settings screen (units toggle works; the player picker switches the replayed match),
  with "Play together" opening the signed-out Together screen, as in the app.
- **Insights** — stroke chips, metric tabs, summary, chart, by-stroke bars and sessions.
- **Muse** — its own tab, as in the app since the Nov 3 restructure (tabs: Live, Score, Muse, Insights, Settings), in
  the app's dark "Lab" style: best change, drill, memory, **What if** (3D swing stage with path trail and ghost),
  **Practice plan**, **Scout yourself** and **Review queue**. The plan, scout and review texts are written by a
  template from the replay's own numbers, labelled "Demo engine · offline".

Three things are not in the app and live outside the phone: the player picker, 1×/2×/4× speed and "Skip to end".

## Source video viewer and timing

The side panel has a **Source video** card: the real broadcast, played from YouTube next to the replay. Nothing is
requested from YouTube until the visitor presses *Load the source video* (the player is `youtube-nocookie.com`;
all 9 videos allow embedding). *Follow the replay* (on by default) makes the **video the clock**: the replay position is read from the player, so the
two cannot drift. Start Session plays both and End Session pauses both (resume continues from the same moment). If the
video buffers or the viewer pauses it, the replay freezes with it; pressing play on a stopped video starts the replay; and
scrubbing the video moves the replay (and its hit feed) to match. Between tracked windows the dead air is skipped. A tap
on any recent hit jumps the video to it (and turns Follow off). It follows at 1x and 2x (YouTube's maximum rate); at 4x the
video pauses and the replay runs alone. "Open on YouTube" links to the same moment.

Every hit carries `video_t`, its time in the source video in seconds (Ostrava: clip start frame + hit frame at 25 fps;
predicted matches: window start `t0_s` + hit frame / 25). Within a tracked window the replay clock and video time
advance together, so the page maps `video = clock + offset` per window. Sessions run in match order.

How well it lines up, measured:

- **Data vs picture** (`tools/f3tennis_model/swing_alignment.py`): the frame where the hitter's racket moves fastest
  falls a median 1-2 frames (40-80 ms) after the data's hit frame in all 8 predicted matches, 76-89% within 3 frames,
  against +1 frame (96% within 3) for the human-labelled Ostrava reference. The data's hit times land on the visible
  swing about as well as human labels do.
- **Data vs audio** (`tools/f3tennis_model/align_check.py`): ball-hit sounds cluster tightly around the data's hits
  (Wimbledon 90%, Shelton 77%, Alcaraz 62%, Sabalenka 59%, against 5-11% by chance), so there is no gross offset. The
  sound arrives 0.1-0.28 s after the picture's hit by a different amount per broadcast (audio delay and mic distance), which
  is why no audio offset is applied; the other matches were inconclusive (crowd and commentary noise).
- **Video vs replay**: they are locked by construction while following. Measured on a live session, video position minus
  replay clock is 0.00-0.02 s throughout at 1x, and the replay ran at 1.95x against a 2x player at 2x. After a seek the page
  checks where the video landed and re-seeks up to twice (a seek can land a few tenths off), keeping the replay still until
  the picture is there, so a window's first moments wait for the video instead of running ahead of it.
- **Racket swing pace** (Emulator controls, outside the phone): *Slower* (default) stretches each swing around contact
  by 1/0.6 so it is easy to follow; *Real time* plays it at the video's speed. The contact instant is identical in both.

An optional per-match `session.video_bias` (seconds) is added to the video time if a picture-based measurement ever shows
a consistent offset. It is 0 for every match today.

## Estimated figures

Footage only gives shot times and a unitless intensity `i` (0-1). Everything else is estimated:

- Swing parameters from `i` and shot index (deterministic): swing = 60 + 90·i km/h; face = ±8·i°
  (sign alternates); path = 10 + 20·i° up (slice: 8-18° down on every third shot below i = 0.25);
  contact is an **assumption**, not data: bell-shaped around the sweet spot with sigma 2.0 + 0.5·i cm
  (0.9× across, 1.1× along), about 85% of hits inside the 4 cm sweet spot (82-88% per player) (sweet iff within 4 cm). Video cannot
  show where the ball met the strings, so Insights' contact and off-center results reflect this prior only.
- Ball speed, spin rpm and spin type: a JavaScript port of
  [`ShotSimulator`](../apple/RacketKit/Sources/RacketKit/ShotSimulator.swift) (acor 0.42, spin gain 0.7).
- Racket motion: a port of `SwingTemplate` (`apple/Shared/Coach/SwingFilm.swift`), using each stroke's own shape
  (forehand, backhand from the other side, overhead serve, short volley). Live turns the racket about a point 0.3 m
  from the butt, as the app's IMU view does, easing to a ready pose between hits and moving the camera to each
  stroke's viewpoint. For labelled hits the swing's timing is that hit's own SAM track in real time; for the rest it
  is the template's profile, slowed to 0.3×. Gyro °/s is the animated rate; g is a spike at contact scaled by `i`.
  In the 8 unlabelled matches every hit is "Hit" and drawn as a forehand.
- What if: baseline = mean of shots so far; levers and limits match `WhatIf.Deltas`; the sentence matches
  `WhatIf.describe`.
- Muse: the suggested questions and the "Find it" button run local ports of `get_session_digest`, `query_shots`,
  `list_shots` and `simulate_change`; a template writes the reply. It does not call Muse Spark and the page says so.

## Schema (`emulator_sessions.json`)

`{"players": [{"name", "video_url", "session"}]}`, written by
[`tools/sam_players_to_emulator.py`](../tools/sam_players_to_emulator.py) over per-window
caches converted with [`tools/sam_track_to_session.py`](../tools/sam_track_to_session.py).
Fields per shot: `t_s`, `kind`, `side` (+ `side_source`), `intensity` (unitless 0-1),
`track_cover`, `clip`. Each session carries `provenance` (player, source, video URL),
`units_note`, `time_note`, and `omitted`.

The labelled entry ([`tools/f3set_to_emulator.py`](../tools/f3set_to_emulator.py), tested by
`tools/test_f3set_emulator.py`) adds per hit: `stroke` (forehand/backhand/serve/volley, as the app's `ShotType`),
`technique`, `hitter` (near/far), `court`, `dir`, `outcome` (in/winner/forced-err/unforced-err), and, when the
hitter's racket was tracked, `prog` (25 values from -1 to +1: how far through the stroke the racket is each frame
from -12 to +12 around contact, by path length) and `path_deg` (direction of the racket centre at contact, scaled by 0.3 and clamped to -15..30 because the camera looks down and inflates upward motion). 50 of the 60 hits have a usable track; the other 10 still carry their real stroke type and
use the template's timing. F3Set video is 25 fps. `data/external/` is not committed; only this derived entry is.

The model-predicted entries (`tools/model_events_to_emulator.py`, tested by `tools/test_model_events.py`) have the same
fields with `predicted: true`, `side_source: "model_prediction"`, `conf` (the model's stroke-type confidence), and
`technique`/`outcome` null. 66% of their hits have a usable hitter's-racket track (`prog`); the rest keep the predicted
stroke type and use the template's timing.

````````

````````markdown
> **Historical.** This is the plan from the first build day. The hardware, AI model and protocol have changed
> since (LSM6DSV320X IMU, Meta Muse Spark, on-racket shot analysis). Current state: [README](../README.md),
> [wiring](WIRING.md), [firmware](../firmware/README.md), [BLE protocol](../firmware/include/protocol.h).

# Tennis Buddy: Hackathon Plan

**Time:** 12:18 to 6:00 (about 5.5 hours). **Team:** CS (apps), EE (wiring + firmware), ME (hardware + calibration + data).
**Requirement:** fork an open-source project ([AahanPrajapati/Smart-Tennis-Racket](https://github.com/AahanPrajapati/Smart-Tennis-Racket), MIT) and add a **trick** and a **treat**.

> **Status (1:20):** firmware, RacketKit, iPhone/Mac/Watch apps, Llama coach (swapped from Gemma; not yet re-verified on device), iCloud sync, app icon
> and Watch drills are built and pushed. Waiting on hardware bring-up. After that, work through [TODO.md](TODO.md).

- **Trick:** the racket itself. Sensors in the handle detect every shot and measure swing speed, ball speed, spin, face angle, swing path and where the ball hit the strings.
- **Treat:** the analytics. iPhone + Mac apps with identical features, an Apple Watch companion, and an on-device **Llama 3.2 3B** coach that explains your session in plain language (open-weights prize category).

How we extend the original project:

| Original "future enhancement" | Tennis Buddee |
|---|---|
| Mobile app for real-time graphs | iPhone, Mac and Watch apps |
| ML to classify strokes | Forehand / backhand / serve / volley detection |
| Force sensors for impact force | High-g accelerometer + impact physics |
| Wi-Fi to a second ESP32 | Bluetooth LE straight to the phone |
| Green/red LED for intensity | Green/red flash on the shot card + Watch haptics |

---

## 1. Hardware

| Part | Role | Settings |
|---|---|---|
| Seeed XIAO ESP32C3 | MCU + BLE (external U.FL antenna at the butt flange) | |
| MPU6050 (GY-521) | Gyro (orientation, rotation) + low-g accel | 1 kHz, ±2000 °/s, ±16 g, DLPF 188 Hz |
| Adafruit H3LIS331DL | High-g accel: swing (MPU6050 saturates at 16 g) + impact | 1 kHz, ±200 g |
| INMP441 | Impact sound (stretch, not in v1 firmware) | 16 kHz I2S |
| 1S LiPo + power button | Button cuts battery power, so **it only charges while switched ON** | |

Positions from the CAD file (measured from the outer face of the butt flange): XIAO 0–30 mm (USB-C at the butt face),
H3LIS331 center 18 mm, MPU6050 chip 39 mm, mic 55 mm (deep end, facing into the handle). The battery sits past the insert:
wrap it in foam so it can't rattle.

### Pin map (EE)

| XIAO pin | GPIO | Connects to |
|---|---|---|
| 3V3 | | VCC of MPU6050, H3LIS331 (VIN), INMP441 VDD |
| GND | | All grounds, INMP441 L/R |
| D4 | GPIO6 | SDA: MPU6050 SDA + H3LIS331 SDA |
| D5 | GPIO7 | SCL: MPU6050 SCL + H3LIS331 SCL |
| D0 / A0 | GPIO2 | Battery voltage: BAT+ → 220 kΩ → A0 → 220 kΩ → GND (optional) |
| D6 | GPIO21 | INMP441 SCK (stretch) |
| D7 | GPIO20 | INMP441 WS (stretch) |
| D10 | GPIO10 | INMP441 SD (stretch) |
| BAT+ / BAT− pads | | Battery through the power button |

I2C addresses: MPU6050 `0x68` (AD0 low), H3LIS331 `0x18` (Adafruit default). No interrupt pins needed.

---

## 2. Architecture

```
Racket (ESP32C3) ──BLE, raw 1 kHz──► iPhone or Mac app ──WatchConnectivity──► Apple Watch
                                       └─ RacketKit (shared Swift package):
                                          decode → orientation → shot detection → metrics → SwiftData
                                       └─ Llama 3.2 3B (MLX Swift, on device) → coach text
```

- **Firmware does no math.** It reads both IMUs at 1 kHz and streams raw samples. All analysis lives in Swift.
- **One device connects to the racket at a time** (iPhone at the court, Mac for the demo).
- **Simulated racket** in the app generates realistic swings and impacts, so the apps can be built and demoed without hardware.
- **Record/replay:** every session's raw data can be saved and replayed, so stats get tuned at a desk.

### BLE protocol (v1)

Service `7E5B0001-6B1D-4D8E-9C1A-7E5B7E5B0001`

| Characteristic | UUID suffix | Props | Payload |
|---|---|---|---|
| IMU stream | `...0002` | notify | Header + 8 samples (below) |
| Status | `...0003` | read, notify (every 2 s) | `u16 battery_mV, u8 fw_major, u8 fw_minor, u8 flags, u8 h3lis_range, u16 dropped` |
| Control | `...0004` | write | `0x01` start stream, `0x02` stop, `0x10 n` H3LIS range (0=100 g, 1=200 g, 3=400 g) |

IMU packet (little-endian, 152 bytes): `u16 seq, u32 t0_us, u8 count(=8), u8 flags`, then 8 samples of
`i16 ax, ay, az, gx, gy, gz` (MPU6050 raw) + `i16 hx, hy, hz` (H3LIS331 raw, 12-bit left-aligned).
Samples are 1 ms apart, starting at `t0_us`. Scales: MPU accel 2048 LSB/g, gyro 16.4 LSB/(°/s); H3LIS at ±200 g = 98 mg/digit after `>> 4`.

---

## 3. Stats (RacketKit)

| Stat | Method | Tier |
|---|---|---|
| Live 3D orientation | Mahony filter on gyro; accel correction only when near 1 g; yaw recenter button | Core |
| Shot detection | High-g impact spike (>8 g jump in < 3 ms) during a fast swing (gyro > 300 °/s) | Core |
| Shot type | Rotation direction about the vertical + face orientation, mirrored for handedness; serve = racket above head before contact | Core |
| Swing speed | Peak angular speed × effective radius (calibrated, default 1.1 m), checked against slow-mo | Core |
| Face angle, swing path | Racket orientation and velocity direction at contact | Core |
| Sweet spot + hit location | Side-to-side: roll-rate jump at impact. Tip vs throat: frame ringing energy (120–200 Hz) at the butt + handle jolt sign. Thresholds from the drop-grid calibration | Core |
| Ball speed | `v_ball ≈ e·v_in + (1+e)·V_racket`, e ≈ 0.4 at the sweet spot (less off-center), v_in ≈ 12 m/s assumed for groundstrokes, ≈ 0 for serves | Nice |
| Spin (rpm) | Racket velocity along the string face at contact → `rpm ≈ k·v_t / r_ball`, k fitted to slow-mo | Nice |
| Session: count, mix, heat map, consistency, fatigue trend | Aggregates over shots | Core / Nice |

Racket constants (edit after the ME measures): mass 325 g, length 686 mm, balance ~320 mm, string-bed center ~520 mm from the butt.

---

## 4. Apps (iPhone + Mac identical, one SwiftUI codebase)

Tabs (iPhone) / sidebar (Mac): **Live · History · Insights · Racket**, plus first-launch setup.

- **Live:** Start/Stop, live 3D racket, a shot card per hit (type, swing speed, ball speed, spin, impact dot) with a green/red edge flash, a running strip (shots, sweet spot %, average speed). Mac: full-screen presenter mode.
- **History:** sessions list → session summary (shot mix, averages per stroke, impact heat map filtered by stroke) → shot detail.
- **Insights:** trend charts across sessions, fatigue chart, **Coach** (Llama summary + "Ask your stats" chat).
- **Racket:** connection, battery, sensor health, **Calibration mode** (hold still → tip up → lay flat → drop-grid with tap-to-label), recorder (raw record/replay, CSV export), simulated racket toggle.
- **Storage:** SwiftData, synced iPhone ↔ Mac with CloudKit (paid developer account).

### Watch (non-playing wrist)

- Start a tennis **workout** from the Watch → starts the racket session on the iPhone; heart rate + calories saved to Health.
- **Haptics per shot:** crisp tap = sweet spot, double buzz = mishit.
- **Last-shot glance:** speed, spin, impact dot.
- **Point logging** (Nice): tap Won / Lost after each point → "win % when first serve > X".
- **Drill mode** (Nice): Llama picks a drill from your weak spots, the Watch counts it down.
- Later: wear the Watch on the hitting wrist for a wrist-lag metric.

### Llama 3.2 3B (on device, MLX Swift)

1. **Session coach** (Core): stats JSON → short report with 2–3 tips.
2. **Ask your stats** (Nice): chat; the app answers from computed stats passed into the prompt.
3. **Drill planner → Watch** (Nice).
4. **Voice journal** (Stretch): audio input.

Model weights are not in git; the app downloads them from Hugging Face on first load. Pre-load them on the demo iPhone and Mac.
Fallback if MLX won't run in our iOS app: llama.cpp with a GGUF build.

---

## 5. Schedule

| Time | EE | ME | CS |
|---|---|---|---|
| 12:30–1:15 | Wire on the bench per the pin map; flash `firmware/`; check serial output | Measurements; tape a 3×3 grid on the strings; foam-wrap the battery | Plan, firmware, Xcode project, simulated racket |
| 1:15–2:30 | Get BLE streaming to the app; fix dropouts | Install electronics in the handle; antenna flat against the flange | Live 3D racket on real data; recorder |
| 2:30–3:30 | Help collect data | Desk calibration, 45 grid drops (tap-to-label), shadow swings, all filmed at 240 fps | Shot detection, swing speed, shot type, sweet spot |
| 3:30–4:30 | Mic (stretch) or help ME | Hit into a blanket or at the wall; slow-mo for speed and spin checks | History, Insights, Watch, Llama coach |
| 4:30–5:30 | Bug fixes | Accuracy slide: app numbers vs slow-mo | Polish, README, backup demo video |
| 5:30–6:00 | Everyone: rehearse the demo, submit | | |

## 6. Calibration (mostly indoors)

1. **Desk (2 min):** app-guided: hold still → tip up → lay flat face-up. Sets gyro bias and maps sensor axes to racket axes.
2. **Drop grid (15 min):** hold the racket face-up with a relaxed grip; drop a ball from ~1.5 m onto each of 9 squares, 5 times each. Tap the square in the app before each drop.
3. **Shadow swings (15 min):** forehands, backhands, serves; film from the side at 240 fps. The racket (686 mm) is the ruler for speed.
4. **Blanket/wall hits (20 min):** draw a line around the ball; rpm = 14,400 ÷ frames per full turn at 240 fps.

## 7. Demo script (3 min)

1. The problem + the forked project (10 s on what we started from).
2. Live: swing the racket → 3D racket moves on the Mac; hit a ball into a blanket → shot card with green flash, Watch taps.
3. Session summary + heat map; Llama coach reads it out in plain language, fully offline.
4. Accuracy slide (app vs slow-mo). Backup: recorded session replay + video.
````````

````````markdown
# Tennis Buddee: Privacy Policy

_Last updated: November 2, 2026_

Tennis Buddee works with a sensor inside your tennis racket to measure your shots.

- **What it collects:** motion and impact-sound results from your racket (over Bluetooth), the shots and sessions
  computed from them, and, if you allow it on Apple Watch, heart rate and active calories during a tennis workout.
- **Where it's stored:** on your devices. If you're signed in to iCloud, sessions sync between your own devices
  through your private iCloud database. We (the developers) cannot see that data.
- **Accounts (optional):** if you sign in with Apple or Google, your profile, friends, and the matches, points and
  racket summaries you choose to share are stored in our Supabase database so your friends can see them.
- **Meta Muse Spark (optional):** when you ask a question, the app sends the question and only the shot or session
  statistics Muse asks for to Meta, through our server. Player notes are sent only while "Let Muse use these notes"
  is on. Health data is never sent. Turn Muse off in Insights to keep everything on the device.
- **Meta Ray-Ban Display (optional):** live shot numbers are sent from your phone to your own glasses.
- **Health data** is used only to show your workout stats and is saved to Apple Health only with your permission.
  It is never used for advertising or shared with anyone.
- **No ads, analytics or tracking.**
- **Deleting data:** delete sessions in the app's History tab, or delete the app. Remove iCloud data in
  Settings → [your name] → iCloud → Manage Storage. To delete your account and shared data, open an issue below.

Questions: open an issue at https://github.com/QuentinL-eng/Tennis-Buddy-Smart-Racket/issues
````````

````````markdown
# Video and racket sensor research

This is a research pipeline, not a validated shot classifier. SAM 3.1 finds candidate racket boxes in sampled video frames. A reviewer labels contacts and shot types, then the export pairs those events with synchronized sensor windows. SAM boxes are 2-D observations; they do not measure 3-D pose, spin, ball outcome, or ground-truth shot type. The highest-confidence candidate can be the wrong racket when multiple players are visible.

## Setup

From the repository root, install Python packages in a virtual environment:

```sh
python3 -m venv .venv
.venv/bin/pip install numpy opencv-python openai
```

Set `MUSE_API_KEY` or `MODEL_API_KEY` in the environment or the repository's ignored `.env`. SAM requests send frames to Meta and consume API credits. Use only video you are entitled to process. Do not commit source footage, API keys, or private results. `--max-calls` limits each invocation; check current Meta pricing and the account's spend separately. This tool does not enforce an account-wide dollar cap.

## Sample a video

```sh
.venv/bin/python tools/shot_video_pipeline.py track /path/to/video.mov \
  --output /path/to/racket-observations.json --start 0 --end 10 --fps 2 --max-calls 10
```

Each call segments one sampled frame using `sam-3.1`; results are saved after each call and reruns resume. Increase `--max-calls` to process more frames. Use a separate output for every video or configuration. Bounding boxes are in original-frame pixels; `null` means no candidate passed the confidence threshold, not that no racket was present. Inspect the video and predictions before use. The frame time stored here uses nominal frame rate and is approximate for variable-rate video.

## Pair with a phone recording

Follow the phone capture instructions in [DATA_COLLECTION.md](DATA_COLLECTION.md), including the visible sync mark and video. Run `tools/phone_session.py` on that session. Check `sync.json` and synchronization visually; clock alignment is an estimate, and packet loss or inaccurate contact refinement can affect it.

Run `track` on that session's `video.mov`. Review the video and create `events.csv` with **zero-based video frame numbers** and one row per verified contact:

```csv
frame,shot_type,note
240,forehand,reviewed contact
480,backhand,reviewed contact
```

Supported labels are `forehand`, `backhand`, `serve`, `volley`, and `unknown`. Do not label shadow swings or uncertain contacts as confirmed hits. Then:

```sh
.venv/bin/python tools/shot_video_pipeline.py export data/phone/SESSION \
  --events data/phone/SESSION/events.csv \
  --observations data/phone/SESSION/racket-observations.json \
  --output data/phone/SESSION/shot-events.json
```

The JSON records the label, phone-clock contact time, observed box when that exact frame was sampled, and the largest IMU timestamp gap in the window. The adjacent NPZ stores actual samples: `samples` has columns listed in `columns`, and event `i` occupies `samples[offsets[i]:offsets[i+1]]`. Times are relative to contact. The program rejects events outside the video timestamp range or without window coverage; a large internal gap is reported and must be reviewed. Only use these as training labels after checking the video, synchronization, sensor range, and gaps.

## Robot recordings and evaluation

`data/room-2026-10-29/results/manifest.csv` contains tentative run assignments; `alignment.csv` contains robot/IMU alignment diagnostics. Use corrected gyro data and its documented calibration only after checking which runs and alignments are valid. Robot movements are controlled examples, not verified player-shot or ball-outcome labels. To test whether they improve classification, first collect reviewed real-player sessions and split by player and session; compare a model using those sessions alone with one also using robot data. Report per-class results and errors on held-out players. Do not infer ball outcomes without independently observed outcomes.
````````

````````markdown
# Swing film: Muse directs, the renderer draws

A swing film shows **your swing**, then **the change Muse recommends**, then the estimated effect. In the app it is a
live 3D animation on the What-if screen (Insights → Muse → What if): it loops your average forehand, backhand, serve or volley and
the changed swing in slow motion, follows the sliders as you move them, and **Show me the best change** has Muse pick
and test the change, which then sets the sliders and the title. `video/` renders the same thing as an 8-second clip.
Every film looks the same because Muse never makes pixels. Muse (Meta's Muse Spark, through the Meta Model API)
reads the racket's numbers, tests changes with the `simulate_change` tool and returns a small, validated script.
A fixed Remotion scene (`video/src/swingfilm/`) turns that script into video. Meta's API has no video model, and
we would not want one here: a generated video could invent a body, a court or a ball flight the racket never measured.

```
racket shots ──► Muse Spark ──► simulate_change (ShotSimulator) ──► make_swing_film(script) ──► validator ──► renderer ──► MP4
               (picks the change)   (estimates the effect)             (≤ 2 levers, short text)    (rejects)    (fixed look)
```

## Inputs: only the racket

The film is a function of five per-stroke averages the racket already reports, and of the simulator's result:

| Input | Source |
|---|---|
| Swing speed, swing path, face angle | IMU, per shot (`ShotMetrics`) |
| Contact point across and along the strings | IMU + mic, per shot |
| Ball speed and spin before/after | `simulate_change` on the player's own average shot |

No phone camera, no photos, no body model. The arm is a fixed pivot; only the racket moves.

## What Muse may choose (the script)

`make_swing_film` takes exactly these fields. Anything else is rejected.

| Field | Limit |
|---|---|
| `stroke` | `forehand` (clip); in the app also `backhand` (mirrored), `serve` (overhead arc) and `volley` (short punch) |
| `swing_percent` | −15…15, or 0 |
| `face_deg` | −6…6, or 0 (+ opens the face) |
| `path_deg` | −10…10, or 0 (+ is more low-to-high) |
| `contact_x_cm`, `contact_y_cm` | −3…3, or 0 |
| levers changed | 1 or 2, each big enough to see: ≥ 3 %, ≥ 2°, ≥ 1 cm |
| deltas | must equal a `simulate_change` call Muse made in the same conversation, for the same stroke |
| `title` | ≤ 24 characters, no digits |
| `cue` | ≤ 60 characters, no digits: what to feel, in plain words |
| `why` | ≤ 90 characters, no digits |
| words | none of: coach, guarantee, landing, depth, net, injury, pain, always, never |

Every number on screen comes from the racket or the simulator, never from Muse's text. The validator sends a
rejected script back to Muse with the reasons, at most twice; after that no film is made.

## What Muse cannot touch (the look)

These live in `apple/Shared/Views/SwingAnimationView.swift` (app) and `video/src/swingfilm/look.ts` (clip), and
are the same for every film:

- Timing: 3 s **Your swing**, then 3 s **Try this** (2.6 s each in the app) (your swing stays as a faint ghost). The app loops the two halves
  and shows the estimates in the What-if cards; the clip is 1920×1080, 30 fps, 8 s, with a 2 s before/after card.
- One camera, one 3/4 angle, no camera moves. Studio backdrop, brand colours (lime `#DDE85B` on `#0B0C09`),
  carbon racket, lime ball.
- The same swing template and timing; 0.16× slow motion through contact in both halves.
- Fixed label slots: the half playing, the title, and (clip) swing speed, path, face and a contact dot on the string bed.
- Text only in the title, cue and card slots, in the brand fonts. Results are always labelled **Estimated**.
- No music, people, court, ball flight or landing spot. Those aren't measured.

## In the app

`SwingFilmDirector` (`apple/Shared/Coach/SwingFilm.swift`) runs the loop with the app's own tools and validator;
`SwingTemplate` there is the swing math, and `SwingAnimationView` draws it with SceneKit. The script never leaves the
device except as Muse's own tool calls, and nothing is generated when Muse is off or signed out.

## Make a clip

```bash
python3 tools/swing_film.py --sample             # asks Muse; writes video/src/config/swingFilm.json
cd video && npx remotion render SwingFilm out/swing-film.mp4
```

`--sample` uses a demo forehand session (realistic numbers, not a recording). Pass `--shots <file.shots.jsonl>` to use
a real session's forehands.
````````

<!-- TB_REFERENCE {"path": "docs/WALL_SPEED_PROTOCOL.md", "sha256": "601dd7a7a957ed511f2514cb061ac571d937f1037edb0f6f718b90a63b7874d1", "trailing_newline": true} -->
````````markdown
# Wall drill: ground-truth ball speed (about 1 hour, one evening)

**Why.** The app turns the gyro into ball speed with `(1 + e) * R * |ω_yz|`, with `e = 0.42` and `R = effectiveRadiusM = 1.15`
(`ShotAnalyzer.swift`, `Calibration.swift`). That radius dates from the first RacketKit commit (Oct 26), before the 2x
gyro error was found, so every displayed swing and ball speed is suspect. This drill measures real ball speed so the
radius can be fitted instead of guessed. It also gives a first labeled set of hard, real shots.

(`docs/WALL_SPEED_TEST.md` is a sibling version of this test, written for `tools/wall_speed_fit.py`: 8-10 m from the
wall, flight time counted by hand from 240 fps video, audio as a fallback. This document is the audio-timed variant,
and `tools/wall_speed_analyze.py` automates the audio timing and writes the truth file that `wall_speed_fit.py` reads.
Both use the same truth-file format, so results from either can be fitted together. A longer distance gives better
timing resolution but a bigger drag bias: expect the mean flight speed to read several percent low at 4 m and
noticeably more at 9 m, and compare fitted radii only between recordings taken at the same distance.)

**What it measures.** For each hit: the racket's pop (loudest sound, matched to the IMU's high-g spike), then the
wall thud. Mean ball speed = wall distance / flight time. The analysis fits that against the IMU's `|ω_yz|`.

## You need
- The racket on **firmware 1.6** (serial status line must say `gyro ±4000 dps`).
- The Mac app (recording to `~/Documents/Recordings`) or any build that writes a `.tbrec`.
- A phone to film, with working audio (normal video at 60 fps is fine; slow-mo audio is unreliable). Tripod or a stable surface.
- A flat, solid wall with nothing breakable, tape measure, chalk or tape, 15+ tennis balls, a notebook.
- Eye protection. Balls come back fast: clear the area behind and beside you.

## Setup
1. Stick a tape cross on the wall at about 1 m height. Mark a hitting spot **4.0 m** from the wall (measure from the
   spot where the ball leaves the racket, in line with the cross). Write the real distance down.
2. Put the phone on the floor or a stand next to you, about 1 m from the hitting spot, mic facing the wall, filming the
   wall and you. Note the distance to the phone.
3. Before hitting anything, **start recording in the app** and check the file grows:
   `ls -l ~/Documents/Recordings/*.tbrec` twice, a few seconds apart. (Last time a 2-hour recording only worked
   because the recorder was already on; do not assume.)
4. Start the phone video.

## Start-of-session checks (1 minute)
- Hold the racket still for 5 s, flat on a table.
- Lift it, rotate it 90° to tip-up, hold 5 s, lay it flat again. Repeat 3 times. (A later self-check will compare the
  gyro with gravity from these; nothing needs doing with them tonight.)
- Tap the handle 3 times, hard. This marks the start in both IMU and audio.

## The drill: self-fed drop hits
Drop the ball so it bounces once off the floor, then hit it at the wall. No ball is coming at the racket, which is
exactly the case the model assumes (`incomingBallMs = 0`). Let the return go; do not hit it.

Effort levels, **interleaved** in this order, so effort is not confounded with time in the session:
- **E** easy: just pop it onto the wall.
- **M** medium: normal rally pace.
- **H** hard: as hard as you can still keep it on the tape cross.

Round = E M H E M H E M H (9 hits). Do **5 rounds of forehands (45 hits)**, then **3 rounds of backhands (27 hits)**.
Rest between rounds, collect the balls. Write down the effort order exactly as hit, and the number of any shot that
was a miss (mishit, bad bounce, ball hit the floor or a side wall, a double hit). Count shots as the app does.

Rules that matter:
- One hit per drop; wait until the ball has stopped before the next.
- Hit the sweet spot; aim at the cross. Do not slice or kick them yet, only flat.
- No shadow swings, taps or tosses between hits that would make a sound near the racket.
- If someone talks or music plays, expect lost shots. Keep it quiet.

End with 3 handle taps, then stop the video and stop the recording.

## Part 2: rally hits (a second, separate recording)
The drop hits above have no incoming ball, so they cannot tell the app's current formula from the "impulse" model in
`tools/wall_speed_fit.py` (ball speed from how much the racket slows at contact): with a still ball the racket's
slowdown is proportional to its speed, and the impulse model's two constants cannot be told apart. To test it the incoming ball must
vary, so do a second recording:
- Hit the wall; let the ball come back off the wall (one floor bounce), and hit it again. Keep the contact point
  within about 0.5 m of your mark so the wall distance holds.
- 30 hits, forehands, effort E M H interleaved as before; mixing short and long returns is good (varied incoming
  speed is the point). Note any hit that was off the mark or a miss.
- Do it as its own recording and its own video (start the recorder and the phone again, with the same 3 handle taps
  at the start and end), so the analysis runs on it separately.

## Collect
- `~/Documents/Recordings/session-….tbrec` (the one that grew).
- The phone video (`.mov`/`.mp4`).
- Your notes: the wall distance, phone distances, effort order, miss numbers.
Keep the raw files until the fit is done, then keep only the CSV result (Mac disk is tight).

## Analyse
Run each recording (drop hits, then rally hits) through the timing script. It also writes the two files that
`tools/wall_speed_fit.py` reads, with the same hit numbering (hit N there is shot N here):
```bash
python3 tools/wall_speed_analyze.py ~/Documents/Recordings/session-….tbrec drill.mov \
    --distance 4.0 --phone-to-contact 1.0 \
    --effort "E M H E M H ... (all shots, in order)" --exclude 7,23 --csv wall_speed.csv \
    --session-csv drill_session.csv --truth-csv drill_truth.csv

python3 tools/wall_speed_fit.py drill_session.csv drill_truth.csv      # add --gyro-scale 0.5 for firmware 1.5
```
Check the timing script first without real data: `python3 tools/wall_speed_analyze.py --selftest`.

Which fit to trust:
- **Drop recording:** the current-formula fit (model A) is the only meaningful one. Its radius is the number to compare with 1.15.
- **Rally recording:** the impulse model (B) can only be judged here. Compare its leave-one-out error with A's, and
  distrust a B whose radius is far from A's or has a huge error bar: that means the two constants are not separable.
- The session CSV holds the raw gyro. The fit's `--gyro-scale` must match what you used here.

## Reading the result
- **Matched shots.** The first line should show nearly every IMU impact paired with a pop. If many are lost, the audio
  was too noisy or too quiet: redo that round.
- **`k` vs 1.633.** The app currently predicts ball speed = 1.633 × |ω_yz|. If your fitted `k` is within about 10% of
  that, the radius is fine. If not, set `effectiveRadiusM = k / 1.42` (more if you correct for drag, below).
- **R².** Above about 0.8 means a single radius is a reasonable model. A low R² or a large intercept means the
  model is structurally off (handle motion, off-centre hits): do not just retune the radius, report it.
- **By effort.** If easy shots fit but hard shots do not, the problem is hard swings (saturation, handle translation).

## Known limits
- Mean speed over the flight is lower than the speed just after contact because of drag, typically 5-10% over 4 m.
  Treat the fitted radius as a slight underestimate. A shorter distance (3 m) lowers this and raises timing error.
- The path length is longer than the wall distance if you hit at an angle. Aim straight at the cross.
- Audio timing assumes the pop and the thud are the two loudest sounds near each hit. Floor bounces are quieter.
- 70 shots from one player tells you the radius for your swing only.
````````

#### Reference: `docs/WALL_SPEED_TEST.md`

<!-- TB_REFERENCE {"path": "docs/WALL_SPEED_TEST.md", "sha256": "88c723bc068aed040d6ad10709bebf045e18b584b071a30b461875175be36969", "trailing_newline": true} -->
````````markdown
# Wall speed test

Ground truth for the ball-speed constants (`effectiveRadiusM`, `ImpactModel.impulseGain`), fitted with
`tools/wall_speed_fit.py`. About 30 minutes, one person plus a phone (a helper makes it easier).

**Setup.** A flat, solid wall: hard-court practice wall or a closed garage door. Mark a hitting line 8–10 m from it
and measure the distance from the contact point to the wall with a tape (note it to ±5 cm). Firmware 1.6 or later
(true gyro scale; older sessions need `--gyro-scale 0.5`). Start an app session recording before the first hit.

**Hits.** 3 effort levels (easy / medium / hard) × 15 hits, flat forehands from a self-feed (drop and hit) so the
incoming speed is near zero for some, plus a few off the rebound so it varies. Pause ~2 s between hits so the
detector's 0.6 s refractory never merges two. A missed or framed hit still counts as an impact: note it.

**Timing, video (preferred).** Phone on a tripod side-on, ~5 m away, framing both the contact point and the wall,
240 fps slow-motion. In a frame-stepping player, count frames from contact (ball leaves the strings) to the ball
touching the wall: flight time = frames / 240. One frame is 4 ms, ~1.5 % at 0.3 s.

**Timing, audio (fallback).** Record audio near the hitter; the time between the string "pop" (coincides with the
IMU impact spike) and the wall thud is the flight time, minus sound travel back from the wall (distance / 343 m/s,
~26 ms at 9 m: subtract it).

**Matching.** Detected impacts are numbered 1, 2, 3… in session order. Start each set with one deliberate, filmed bounce hit
straight down as a marker (it is an impact too: note its number); then number video hits in the same order and drop rows for hits the detector missed. The tool prints how many
impacts it found: it must match your count.

**Truth file.** `hit,distance_m,flight_time_s` (or `hit,ball_speed_ms` from a radar). distance/time is the mean
speed over the flight, a few percent below the exit speed (drag), so constants fit slightly low.

**Record also.** Racket (model, string tension), handle hardware version, grip firmness (loose / normal / tight:
grip changes the effective mass), effort level per hit, wall type, indoor/outdoor.

**Safety.** Nobody between hitter and wall or near the rebound line; eye protection for the hitter on hard hits at
short range; check the wall/door can take it and nothing breakable is behind or beside it.

**Run.** `python tools/wall_speed_fit.py session.csv truth.csv` (needs ≥ 8 hits). Try `--demo` first.
````````

````````markdown
# "What if" tool-use dataset for Muse Spark

Synthetic conversations that teach Muse to test a technique change instead of only describing a session. Muse
reads the digest, proposes a change ("close the face 3°, swing 5% slower"), calls `simulate_change`, and reports
the estimated result. Every tool result in the dataset is what the app would return, because the physics and tool
code are mirrored from Swift (`ml/coach_sim.py`, checked against `ShotSimulator.swift` output in the tests).

```bash
python3 ml/whatif_synth.py priors                     # real recordings -> ml/whatif_priors.json (needs the local data)
python3 ml/whatif_synth.py generate                   # -> data/whatif/ (400 players, seed 7, ~8 s)
python -m unittest discover -s ml -p test_whatif_synth.py
```

`ml/whatif_priors.json` is in git (summary numbers only, 8 KB), so `generate` works without the raw recordings.

## What the real data contributes

| Source | Quality | Used for |
|---|---|---|
| `data/phone/` TennisCamera sessions, Oct 28 (45 camera-confirmed hits, ~25% packet loss) | good | Racket speed at contact (median 120 km/h) and its shot-to-shot spread (CV 0.14) |
| `data/sessions/*/positions.csv`, 274 reviewed contacts | good | Shape of the contact cloud; the ridge model's 1.83 cm error for mic-only hits |
| `data/club-2026-10-28/` raw-stream CSVs (17% of the stream arrived) | bad | Rally cadence, per-recording BLE throughput, the gyro clipping in 8 of 11 recordings, 27 real swings (median 75 km/h) |

The club data can't measure strokes, but it does describe the conditions the agent has to cope with. Each synthetic
session gets club-like or phone-like link conditions. With a club-like link, a shot that comes before the previous
448-sample window has finished sending becomes a mic-only hit (21% of club-like shots, against 7% on a phone-like
link). With the gyro range bug, swings above 144 km/h are saturated. In 4% of sessions the motion stream never
comes up at all. In each case Muse has to say it can't simulate, rather than invent a baseline.

**Assumed, not measured:** swing path and face angle per stroke (no recording has orientation yet), the shot
mixes, and the injected technique flaws. The lab contacts were thrown across the face on purpose (median 4.8 cm
off), so on-court contact uses that shape scaled by 0.55–1.0. The result is 46% of motion shots in the sweet spot.

## Generated files (`data/whatif/`, git-ignored)

- `conversations_{train,val,test}.jsonl`: 2,263 examples split by player (80/10/10), in OpenAI chat format with
  `tools` (the same schemas as `CoachTools.schemas`, including the racket and memory tools). The first two messages
  are exactly what `MuseCoach` sends for a question (system prompt, then the question with no data), and Muse's
  first move is to call `get_session_digest` itself. `metadata` holds the
  ground truth: the injected flaw, whether the chosen change addresses it (`flaw_found`, 77%), link conditions
  and units.
- `whatif_table.csv`: 85,552 simulated changes (baseline, deltas, before/after, whether each passes the
  guardrail and reaches the target, and which one was chosen). Use it for evals or to train a ranker.
- `shots.csv`, `sessions.csv`, `players.jsonl`: the synthetic shots, session conditions, and player truth.
- `manifest.json`: counts, seed, and a hash of the priors.

## Example kinds

| Kind | Count | What Muse learns |
|---|---:|---|
| `objective` | 1,326 | A goal (more spin, more pace, cleaner contact, slice→topspin). It tests the best single change on two levers in parallel, then a combination if needed, and picks the **smallest change that reaches the target**. The pick is guided by what the digest shows (an open face points to closing the face; a flat path to swinging more low-to-high). |
| `player_whatif` | 465 | The player proposes the change (e.g. "open the face 3° and swing 5% slower"). Muse runs exactly that and says whether it's worth it. |
| `player_whatif_extreme` | 122 | The request is beyond the tool's limits. Muse reports the capped change and suggests a smaller step. |
| `unmodeled` | 222 | Questions about depth or net clearance. Muse reports speed and spin and says flight isn't modeled. |
| `contact_spread` | 83 | The average contact is already centered. Muse explains that the issue is scatter, which the simulator can't model. |
| `no_motion`, `*_error` | 45 | Mic-only or saturated data. Muse says it can't simulate, with no made-up numbers. |

Every final answer is under 80 words and calls the result an estimate, and the tests check that every number in it
appears in a tool result.

## Caveats

- ShotSimulator is a sensitivity model. The ball speeds it gives are high for the racket speeds (median forehand:
  95 km/h racket, 143 km/h ball). The dataset teaches Muse to use the tool honestly; it doesn't make the tool right.
  Recalibrating `acorCenter` from the TennisCamera ball tracks was attempted and is blocked: in session
  `10-29-26-1005`, most post-impact track windows sit near 0 km/h (static and second balls poison the tracks) with a
  few wild outliers, so no trustworthy launch-speed fit exists yet, and no constant was changed. The recalibration
  data now comes from WhatIfTrial instead: the What-if screen stores predicted vs measured ball/spin per change, so
  the slow-swing bias can be fit from completed trials once they accumulate, then `acorCenter` updated and the
  dataset regenerated.
- Face and path changes move spin identically in the model. Which one Muse picks comes from the digest heuristic
  (`diagnosis()` in `whatif_synth.py`), not from the physics.
- Answers are templated, so their wording is repetitive. To vary the wording, paraphrase the final turns with a
  model, keeping every number.
- Once impact-mode club sessions exist, re-run `priors` with their windows added and regenerate.
````````

<!-- TB_REFERENCE {"path": "docs/WIRING.md", "sha256": "19a5e54955b10a9814808c3a7704f33ae0a5294ac531916dadf1d4e846b27885", "trailing_newline": true} -->
````````markdown
# Wiring (as built)

XIAO ESP32C3, viewed from the component side with USB-C at the top.
Left header top→bottom: D0 D1 D2 D3 D4 D5 D6. Right header top→bottom: **5V GND 3V3 D10 D9 D8 D7**.

| XIAO pin | Connects to |
|---|---|
| GND | STEVAL-MKI251A GND (13) + SDO (22), INMP441 GND + L/R |
| 3V3 | STEVAL-MKI251A VDD (1) + VDDIO (2) + OCS (3) + CS (19), INMP441 VDD, SDA/SCL pull-ups (4.7 kΩ each) |
| D4 (GPIO6) | STEVAL-MKI251A SDA (21) |
| D5 (GPIO7) | STEVAL-MKI251A SCL (20) |
| D1 (GPIO3) | INMP441 SCK |
| D2 (GPIO4) | INMP441 WS |
| D3 (GPIO5) | INMP441 SD |
| — | INMP441 L/R → GND |
| BAT+/BAT− pads | Battery through the power button |

The IMU is an LSM6DSV320X (gyro + ±16 g + ±320 g accel) on ST's STEVAL-MKI251A adapter, replacing the earlier
MPU6050 + H3LIS331DL. CS high selects I2C; SDO low sets address 0x6A. **Do not use the 5V pin for the sensors.**
The firmware pin map in `firmware/src/main.cpp` and `firmware/src/mic.cpp` matches this table.

Check it: `cd firmware && pio run -e i2cscan -t upload`, then open the serial monitor. It should report
`0x6A(reg0F=0x73 ...)` on SDA=D4 (the scanner also lists other SCL pins for it; that is the ESP32 leaving the last SCL
pin attached, not a wiring fault). Then reflash the main firmware: `pio run -t upload`.

Mic check: `pio run -e micprobe -t upload`, then open the serial monitor. A connected INMP441 shows a changing level on
slot0 (`-> MIC DETECTED`) that jumps when you clap; slot1 stays 0 because L/R is tied to GND.
````````

#### Reference: `firmware/README.md`

<!-- TB_REFERENCE {"path": "firmware/README.md", "sha256": "90d639f36b7d7cd77afdf37f1a4dbde0d4cb331ac3f2191dff90e728c8d89500", "trailing_newline": true} -->
````````markdown
# Tennis Buddee firmware (EE)

Seeed XIAO ESP32C3 + LSM6DSV320X (on an ST STEVAL-MKI251A adapter). Reads gyro, ±16 g and ±320 g accel at 1 kHz
and streams samples over BLE as
"Tennis Buddy". Pin map: [../docs/WIRING.md](../docs/WIRING.md). Protocol: [include/protocol.h](include/protocol.h).

The INMP441 mic feeds an on-device ML model that reports sweet spot / % off-centre for each hit (serial `SHOT …`
lines and BLE characteristic `…0005`). Docs: [../ml/README.md](../ml/README.md).

## Flash it

```bash
python3 -m pip install --user platformio   # once
cd firmware
~/Library/Python/3.13/bin/pio run -t upload
~/Library/Python/3.13/bin/pio device monitor
```

(If `pio` is on your PATH, just use `pio`.) If upload fails: hold **BOOT**, tap **RESET**, release BOOT, upload again.

## What you should see in the serial monitor (115200)

```
LSM6DSV320X WHO_AM_I = 0x73 (expect 0x73)
LSM6DSV320X: OK
INMP441 mic + sweet-spot model: OK
BLE: advertising as "Tennis Buddy"
rate 1000 Hz | a[g] -0.06 -0.01 -0.99 ... | high-g a[g] 0.0 0.0 -1.2 | mic floor 160 peak 470 trig 1500 hits 0 | ...
```

Checklist:
- **rate ≈ 1000 Hz.** Much lower means I2C trouble: shorten the wires, check pull-ups.
- **Lying flat and still:** one accel axis reads ≈ ±1.00 g; the gyro reads near 0.
- **high-g:** sent in the old H3LIS units, fixed at the ±400 g range since 1.6 (~0.2 g steps; the sensor reads
  ±320 g), so 1 g at rest shows as ≈ ±1.0–1.4 on one axis.
- **mic:** `floor` is the background level, `peak` the loudest sample in the last second; a hit fires when it beats `trig`.
- **NOT FOUND:** check SDA = D4, SCL = D5, 3V3, GND. The LSM6DSV320X must be at 0x6A (SDO to GND, CS to 3V3).
- **Power button** cuts the battery, so the battery only charges while switched ON.
- **Antenna:** plug the U.FL antenna in before testing range; without it, range is a few cm.

## Shots, windows and the backlog (firmware 1.6)

With an app that knows it (`TB_STREAM_IMPACTS_ACKED`, protocol in `include/protocol.h`), each hit goes out as:

1. `TBHit` the moment it is detected.
2. `TBShotSummary` (80 bytes): the whole shot, computed on the racket by `src/shot.cpp`, a port of the app's
   `ShotAnalyzer` that uses the calibration and profile the app sends (`TB_CMD_SHOT_CONFIG`). The app shows the shot
   from this alone.
3. The 448-sample window, as backlog: 56 `TBWindowChunkAcked` that the app acks (`TB_CMD_WINDOW_ACK`). Missing
   chunks are re-requested (`TB_CMD_WINDOW_RESEND`), and unacked windows go again after 5 s.

`src/backlog.cpp` holds up to 6 windows in RAM. When they are all taken (slow link), or no phone is connected and the
racket has been still for 3 s, windows are written to the unused `spiffs` partition (1.375 MB, 117 windows) and
sent oldest first once the link is free, across reboots. Erasing flash stalls the CPU for tens of ms, so it only
happens while the racket is idle; writes go one 256-byte page per loop pass. Once an app has asked for this mode,
the racket also captures windows with no phone connected (flag kept in NVS).

The status line ends with the backlog counters (`acked`, `resent`, flash `waiting` / `spilled` / `lost`), `shot max`
(µs per summary) and free heap.

Apps from before 1.6 still get plain impact mode: windows sent once, no summaries.

## Host tests

```bash
clang++ -std=c++17 -fsanitize=address,undefined -Iinclude -Isrc -o /tmp/backlog_test tools/backlog_test/backlog_test.cpp src/backlog.cpp && /tmp/backlog_test
```

`tools/backlog_test` runs the backlog against a fake flash that, like the real one, can only clear bits between
erases. The shot analyzer is checked against the Swift one by RacketKit's `ShotParityTests` (`swift test` in
`apple/RacketKit`), which builds `tools/shot_parity` itself.
````````
